utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't. Not now. I used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, but back then, on the 16th of April, did you have a car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I may have bought the same model car, maybe a month earlier, a Zastava 750, it's called. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact that the witness whose testimony we have just mentioned, that his testimony was corroborated by Witness Y's testimony, he was heard here on the 29th of September, 1998, and Witness Y does remember the concern of that other witness we've mentioned who, after seeing this group of soldiers around the Kupreskic houses, called some of his friends to talk about it and know what action, what steps had to be taken, given those circumstances. This was not a question, just a comment of mine. I also wanted to remind you that other witnesses came to testify and stated that some Croatian families were transferred, were moved by car in the afternoon or in the early evening of the 15th of April. Do you remember that testimony? This involves, more particularly, the family of Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Is the question whether I recall the testimony of certain witnesses or do I recall that certain Croatian families moved out? Which of the two is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'd like answers to both questions on these two issues. Just let me explain. If you can't remember those testimonies, then I can show you in more detail those testimonies so that you know what to answer on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall that a witness did testify that he saw Ivica driving his family and taking his family out of Ahmici. He only could have seen him driving his wife to Krcevine to see her mother because she had just arrived. I don't know whether he saw them coming back an hour or two later. None of the Kupreskics left that night, until that morning. So it was myself, my brother, my father, our families, Ivica, and that's all, and they were all there at home that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us turn to what you allegedly did on the 16th of April, 1993. I must say that the statements you made as to your movements on the 16th of April do tally with the statements by some of the witnesses we've heard. I don't want to name those witnesses because I can't remember right now whether they were protected or not. They were three Defence witnesses with whom you were for most of that day, on the 16th of April, and who made statements that totally match yours, right into the minute details, so I suppose that you remember that day perfectly as well. Therefore, I'm going to put some very specific questions to you following your testimony. I want to know when, at what time, you were warned of what was about to happen? When were you informed that you had better try and reach a shelter? What time was it then, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I did not recall the exact time. I did not look at a watch; I did not have one. I know it was dark, and based on the time that I spent rousing my parents and then my wife, getting the children ready and getting down to Sakic's, it must have been about 4.00. I said that it was just dawn. It was just dawning. I know about that time, the daybreak. I know because I went to work around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said around 4.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning. As I said, from the time I got up and reached the house of Niko Sakic, I perhaps needed half an hour to 45 minutes. That's an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This is another matter which I fail to understand. Around that hour, you were already alerted to the danger which could happen, which could descend on Ahmici. I'm referring to the testimony of Dragan Vidovic, he was just before you, and he made a statement, and I should like to know why, at that particular moment, didn't you try to alert your neighbours, your friends.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Alert them to what? I had an information that there was a possibility that we may be attacked from Barin Gaj by Muslims. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, it's your question which surprises me. You are warned about imminent danger, that something could happen in the area of Ahmici, and you were asked to go to a shelter. Did you think that because the Muslims were attacking that they would -- did you think that Ahmici Muslims were your enemies, that they would attack you, your co-villagers, that they would attack you? Is that what you thought?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not for a second did I think that the attackers would be Fuad Junuz, and the Muslims that I know. We were all afraid of the word "Mujahedin." After the 20th, in the first days after we came home after the 20th, we did have a couple of such situations where the Mujahedin went to Barin Gaj, but I did not -- I was not afraid of my neighbours at that time. What could my neighbours do to prevent the Mujahedin from doing whatever they wanted to do? In view of the fact that the attack was expected from that direction, it didn't occur to me to call anyone from there, but we just went to seek shelter the way we did before. Of course, we would keep watch too like we usually did and nothing would happen. We were hoping that day too that nothing would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you thought that your Muslim neighbours, your Muslim friends were quite safe. I'm trying to understand. I'm not asking you any questions. I'm simply trying to understand what happened.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if I was even thinking about Muslims at that time. I was hurrying to get my wife and children, to take them to Zume. We had a small baby. They all needed to be taken away. I can't say that I thought of them at the time -- at that time when I got up. Looking back on it from here, I don't know, but at that moment I just wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Because you did time to warn some other people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that the accused would need a break, perhaps of five minutes. He seems very tired to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The accused must say if he is tired. I believe we have reached a very important point and the accused should say if he is tired or if he can go on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I asked you if you had a telephone at home.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And it worked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it worked that morning. I didn't use it, nor did it ring. It didn't ring that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree that one could reasonably assume that your telephone functioned because it was in perfectly good order, and Vlatko Kupreskic's and -- did it ever occur -- you never thought of calling or making a call to your Muslim neighbours? What I don't understand is why did you think there had ever been an attack by Mujahedin forces and that in case of such an attack you would -- your Muslim neighbours would be safe, and they were completely disarmed as you knew they were disarmed. Why is it that you thought there would be no problem, no safety risk for them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time that I got up, I didn't have time to call as you claim. I left as quickly as I could to wake up my brother and my father, and I came back to help my wife get the children ready. I had reason to suspect, perhaps, that people from the outside Mujahedin -- I didn't know whether they would do something bad to the Muslims, to my neighbours. We didn't know what that army was like. We heard that that army, those people, slaughtered, they killed, they burned. Perhaps the Muslims were afraid of them just as we were. The Vitezovi and the PPNs or some army from Zuti, they were as scary to us as they were to the Muslims, and we were just looking to get out of their way. So I just assume that the Muslims tried to stay out of the way of the Mujahedin, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But when you left your house, I imagine that you looked around you, perhaps in the direction of Sakib Ahmic's house, and you could see that that house was very quiet, that everybody was asleep still.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had no need to pass by Sakib Ahmic's house. I was leaving my house. So I was going from my house towards Zume. Sakib's house is towards Ahmici. I had no need. I couldn't even see that house; it was dark. It's 50 to 70 metres away from me. There's a lot of trees, shrubs. So you could see it but only in daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You could not see any other Muslim house when you left your house, your own house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You did not try to see if in one of the Muslim houses nearest to you anybody was awake and getting ready?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any of that, nor did I hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You remember the testimony of your friend that we just talked about, and paragraph 29 of that evidence, of that statement, that on different occasions Zoran and his wife said that they left their house on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, before the attack, and that Zoran also had moved his parents from Ahmici, that he made two trips to take them out because he had a small car. After that he returned to Ahmici. Because it is true that you had a small car. Did you use that car that morning, that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I didn't use it on that day, nor for ten days after that. That story could have only been when I drove my family to Vitez, but not on that day, not on the 16th. This was ten days after the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But wasn't it logical to take the car in order to simply move quicker?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps it was more logical, but I went with my brother, and my father, and the others to the shelter. The shelter was close. I didn't use the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you not to use your car that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Weren't you afraid that your car might have been damaged, destroyed, ransacked in that attack conducted by Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a very -- it's a small Fiat car which had cost 500 German Marks, so it was in the garage of Branko's house, the brother of Josip Livancic. So after that I really wasn't thinking about the car any more. I didn't even think about my house, never mind the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You described soldiers you saw on the road, and in that description which you gave us, I believe you mentioned some armbands that -- and some other witnesses also said that the soldiers they saw on the road were wearing some armbands, but you just did not mention them. You don't remember them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember the armbands until I saw the late Mirjan Santic. I saw the armband on him. But that morning I don't remember whether the army, the soldiers, were wearing them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm now calling upon your military experience that -- in the former JNA too and the experience that you might have gained after that, after the 16th of April. What do these armbands mean? What was the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was just a mark of recognition. I assumed there were uniforms on all sides, so for them not to mix up -- not to get mixed up. There were people without insignia. I assume that this could perhaps have been the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are these armbands still of the same colour? Could you tell us under which circumstances would someone use them, for what kind of recognition?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had never seen them up until the time that I saw it on Mirjan Santic. So I don't know when they are used. So what I said is I just assumed that it was used as a sign of recognition, so that you could tell who was who.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But afterwards, when you became an officer, with all the experience that you acquired later, did you see those armbands used?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see them afterwards because the company that I was in did not use them. We never had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And other companies use such armbands, to your knowledge, and what did they mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a very short film of about a minute, a minute and a half at this point, and we shall also distribute the transcript. It is not very important.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be 376P, and 376A will be the number of the transcript. (Videotape played) "(Voiceover) Interviewer: The lads are just leaving on an assignment under the command of Mirko Cosic, a young man we all know well from the ranks of the Croatian Defence Council. Mirko, this is prime time television, just after the news and everybody is watching. Speak to the people and tell them what the fighting has been like lately. "Soldier wearing a white T-shirt underneath his uniform: Everything is in order. Best regards. Not to worry. All soldiers doing well and in good health. Everything is okay. "Second soldier: Busovaca will never fall... "Soldier wearing a white T-shirt underneath his uniform: It will never fall, never for as long as we live! "Voice in the background: Zoka, would you like some? "Voice in the background: Film that one down there. "Soldier sitting on the ground: Say hello to the neighbours over there. Tell them ... Zijo Zmijanac regards. "Interviewer: Well, they will see you. "Soldier sitting on the ground: ... Dzeto, tell them that. "Voice in the background: Zoka, wants some bacon? "Zoka or interviewer: Not now, later. "Soldier with headband: Some YU rock. "Interviewer: How are things going? "Soldier with headband: Never better. "Interviewer: Your mum will be watching you this evening, why don't you say hello? "Soldier with headband: I will, thanks. Mum, take care of me! "Interviewer: Guys, you will be going on assignment soon. How does it feel to be going into action? You will be going up against the enemy. Are you afraid? "Soldier sitting on the ground, holding a piece of bread: First class! "Interviewer: Aren't you afraid? "Soldier sitting on the ground, holding a piece of bread: No, well ... "Interviewer: Well, do you know what you are fighting for? "Soldier sitting on the ground, holding a piece of bread: Mother of Jesus! Of course we do. "Interviewer: Well, we did help a few Muslims ... look what happened ... "Interviewer: And that is how the young men from the special units spend their time before leaving for the front line, and before going to other positions where they will help their friends and fellow soldiers, the defenders at the defence lines, all of them united, prepared at all times to face the enemy, ready to defend their homeland!"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the date of that again? There was one shown right at the beginning of the clip and I didn't take it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We shall clarify it, Judge. It is not important whether we know the precise date. This was taken after the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, I want an answer, not for you to comment on whether it's important or not. I want a date for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm not commenting, Judge May, I simply was trying to say that we cannot answer straightaway. We have to verify it in order to establish the date as precisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as Defence we were wondering, as the Defence, if we could get information as to where this was filmed. Which locale is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Terrier, could you tell us where this was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I cannot do that. I show this film only to show the witness soldiers wearing those ribbons on their shoulders, which were mentioned by various Muslim witnesses and a number of Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the witness if the ribbon that he saw on Mirjan Santic's shoulder looked like those that we saw in this film.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw in this film white ribbons. Mirjan Santic was wearing a light blue one then when I saw him. I saw similar light blue ones on the 18th, with the military police who had taken us to Pirici, something similar to that. I even remember one of them. I saw one wearing a black scarf on his head, and I remember one of the people up at Pirici was wearing a scarf like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You saw this film. Would you perhaps know where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I should like to talk again about those soldiers that you saw along the road at the time when you were coming back from the shelter. I was rather astonished about what you said last week. You said that you noticed the brilliance of the soldiers, that you experienced something that you never experienced before, and you said that you were terrified, that you wanted to get away from them as quickly as possible. Will you please explain to us why this emotion, such a forceful emotion? Why this terror? Why did you experience this terror at the time when you were threatened by Mujahedin attack, when you were looking for a shelter for your family, and that those soldiers who were there to protect you and guarantee the safety of your families. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that what I saw that morning from that army, I'd never seen anything like that in my life. I'd served my military term of duty in the JNA, and I'd never seen anything like it. They had a shine in their eyes. It wasn't different from the shine in the eyes of the other people, but their faces were black. They were painted black so that in the dark you didn't notice that, but you would remember those eyes which you could see the reflection of them, and it looked horrible to me. I said that I don't remember whether I was carrying a child or whether I was leading my children, but I was trying in every way to get as far away from them as possible. I don't know if I thought at that moment what would happen if they had said to me, "Look, at him. He's an able-bodied man and he's leaving with his wife and children." I just wanted to get away as soon as possible. This was all in passing. It was just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And you, a reserve officer, or at least a reserve officer of the former JNA, you did not dare ask them for any kind of information from the soldiers about what was going on, about possible danger?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't dare ask them. I said this was just in passing and I didn't have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm going now to those fires which you saw. You told us that on the 16th of April you saw houses on fire, but you had no means of knowing which were those houses. Yet, if I understood your testimony properly, neither on the 16th or in the night between the 16th or the 17th or on the 17th, the 17th and the 18th, did you see what was happening. You did not see your house before the 19th of April, is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. You understood me well. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During that time, did you see, or notice, or catch a glimpse of Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw Vlatko only in Vitez, maybe 15 or 20 days later, for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So on the 16th or the 17th or the 18th you never saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What about Ivica Kupreskic? Did you see him one of those days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Ivica on all of those three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I should like you to explain to us why were you in that depression? You told us, and other witnesses before you told us that for a considerable part of that period you stayed in that depression. Could you please remind us of the reasons why you were there? What was your idea? Why did you stay in that place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We stayed in the depression because the shelter was close to us, with the wives and children. We were some 50 to 100 metres away from the shelter. We had information about the attack. We had already seen that the army had gone by. We could hear the shooting. War was being waged up above. Bullets were hitting the branches of the trees. So we were there in case somebody came to threaten the lives of those who were in the shelter, to not allow that, to shoot back, to block them. That was the only reason we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it was a defence line which you set up in order to protect the shelter with your families?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We didn't make any kind of line. We were all together in a group, all five or six of us. We were in a group, one next to another, behind each other. There was no line. We didn't dig any trenches. We were standing next to a rock, a hill, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell us, how long did you think that it was a conflict between Muslim attackers and Croat defenders? How long did you think that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally, during those first few hours, when the shooting was at its most intense, perhaps until the arrival of UNPROFOR or maybe nine or ten hours until the first time I went to see my family, I thought it was true, what we had been told, that it was the Mujahedin, or I don't know who, who had attacked and that the army had taken on the fight and that they were fighting. But then later, in the course of the day, as I could see that houses were burning up above, and they were mostly Muslim houses, and when Ivica said that the Muslim houses around our house were burning, I still don't know whether this was an attack and then this had been a counterattack, or whether it was all one attack, but I could see that the Muslims were getting hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday -- no, sorry, Friday, you spoke about the great suffering of various women and the terror to which those women were subjected. It didn't occur to you that those women might have been Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could assume that they were Muslim because there were no Croat homes there. All the houses there were Muslims. They were fleeing -- in the first -- on the first day, I knew that some were killed by the road, and then I assumed that the others had fled and that there were no casualties on that first day. I assumed that if the houses were burned, perhaps the people had had enough time, that they had escaped, but it turned out that this did not happen to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It was then. What day, what time of the day did you realise that there was not an attack, as the one you had announced, and all that was happening was very different from what you thought before the morning of the 16th of April? At what time, roughly, did you realise what had happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never realised that this had happened, and to this day, I still don't know that this happened. On that very day, I don't remember who started firing first at whom, but already in the afternoon hours of that first day, the 16th, I could see that there were casualties among the Muslims, that their houses and property were being destroyed. To this day, it is not clear to me whether it was the Muslims who had started shooting first or the army, I don't know that, but I could see the outcome, the results of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Counsel Terrier, it is already 1.00, but I should like the Defence counsel not to make any comments or commentaries during the testimony of the accused. Perhaps it has to do with my earphones, but I should very much like to ask them not to comment on the testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
